profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for a systematic review protocol and evidence-extraction template that will evaluate how existing studies of digital health technologies for chronic disease apply health technology assessment (HTA) frameworks. The context is that the team has drafted a DHT-specific HTA mapping matrix and a pilot screening/extraction workflow, and now needs to judge whether the design is ready for reviewer training and pilot testing. The agenda is to review the proposed scope of included technologies, the extraction sheet structure, what will count as 'full HTA coverage' in the review synthesis, and whether the protocol is ready for pilot use. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on using the current review design for the pilot phase, plus a short list of minor adjustments before launch.

members.name: Dr. Priya Nair
members.expertise: Health technology assessment frameworks, reimbursement evidence requirements, evidence synthesis for service adoption decisions
members.background: Priya leads methodological reviews for a regional evidence advisory unit and has spent the last decade adapting conventional HTA frameworks for non-drug technologies, including telehealth and remote monitoring services.
members.private_state: She wants the review design to look rigorous enough to support a later policy-facing paper, and she is worried that if the extraction framework becomes too broad or too interpretive, the team will not be able to make defensible statements about gaps in DHT evidence.
hidden_assumptions: If a study is said to have addressed an HTA domain, it should contain enough explicit evidence to support a real appraisal judgment, not just a passing mention.
Patient-facing interventions are the core unit of interest for DHT-specific HTA, while provider-side infrastructure is background context unless it is itself the intervention.
The 'current extraction sheet' is the revised spreadsheet she last annotated in the shared drive, which already includes ethics, interoperability, and organizational columns.
A review design is 'ready for pilot' when the coding categories are stable enough that disagreements will mostly be clerical rather than conceptual.

members.name: Dr. Mateo Silva
members.expertise: Digital intervention evaluation, systematic review operations, pragmatic trial design for chronic disease technologies
members.background: Mateo is an implementation scientist who has coordinated several reviews of remote care platforms and mobile self-management tools, with a focus on making heterogeneous digital health studies comparable enough for publication.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the design usable for a fast-moving literature base and is concerned that an overly strict HTA interpretation will make most studies look noncompliant in a way reviewers may see as unfair or subjective.
hidden_assumptions: For this review, an HTA domain counts as covered if the study reports any substantive information relevant to that domain, even if it is not enough for formal decision appraisal.
Digital health for chronic disease includes the broader care-delivery stack around the patient intervention, such as clinician dashboards and monitoring hubs, if they are part of the service model.
The 'current extraction sheet' is the version embedded in the latest protocol draft circulated by email, which still uses combined implementation/organizational fields.
A design is 'ready for pilot' once reviewers can start applying it and discover edge cases during pilot extraction, even if some categories will be refined afterward.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the review should identify studies with 'full HTA coverage.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a study addresses the major HTA domains with enough explicit detail that a policy-style appraisal could genuinely judge value, trade-offs, or readiness.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a study touches each major domain somewhere in the paper or supplements, even if the treatment is brief and not appraisal-grade.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and both expect it to signal comprehensiveness; because they are reviewing a mapping framework rather than rating a specific paper live, neither is pushed to operationalize the threshold in the meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of 'digital health technologies for chronic disease'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the review covers 'DHTs that manage chronic disease.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the core inclusion set is patient-facing tools and tightly coupled devices used directly for self-management or monitoring, while clinician-facing platforms are usually part of service organization rather than the DHT under review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the review includes the broader digital care intervention package, including clinician dashboards, triage portals, and monitoring back ends, if they are integral to chronic disease management.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The category label is common in the literature and both have worked with hybrid interventions before; because they each view their boundary as the obvious one, phrases like 'remote monitoring platform' feel mutually intelligible without further unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'current extraction sheet' is being approved
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the current extraction sheet' or 'the matrix in the draft.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of spreadsheet version v3.2 in the shared review folder, where ethics, equity, interoperability, and organizational impact are split into separate columns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the table pasted into the protocol Word draft from two weeks earlier, effectively v2.9, where implementation and organizational considerations are still merged and interoperability is only noted in comments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The versions differ only in a few second-order structural details, and both were circulated recently; since each assumes everyone is naturally working from the most familiar 'latest' artifact, the shared reference seems unambiguous.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design should be 'ready for pilot next week.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the categories, instructions, and edge-case handling are sufficiently settled that the pilot mainly confirms consistency and produces near-final coding guidance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the pilot is precisely where unresolved category boundaries will be discovered and adjusted, so readiness only requires a workable starting structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Pilot phases often serve both validation and refinement, so the phrase feels naturally shared; their difference lies in degree of stability expected before starting, which rarely gets stated unless a timeline conflict emerges.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to be the last substantive design check before we start. If we're saying the design is ready for pilot next week, the categories should already be stable enough that the pilot is really about confirming consistent use, not reopening basic definitions. I also need the matrix to support a defensible synthesis later, ideally something strong enough for a policy-facing paper on where DHT evidence is thin.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I thought we could use this as a final design check on whether the mapping matrix is in a good enough place to support a credible synthesis of the evidence gaps in DHTs that manage chronic disease. For me, the main question is whether we're genuinely ready for pilot next week, or whether there are still any structural issues we need to settle first.

turns.inner_thought: I mainly want to make sure we can start with what we have and refine from there. Ready for pilot next week means the structure is usable, not perfect. And I hope we don't narrow the scope so much that we miss the broader digital care models in chronic disease, because a lot of real interventions include dashboards, coordination layers, and monitoring hubs. Also, when she says the current extraction sheet, I assume we're talking about the matrix in the draft from the protocol email.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. From my side, I mostly want to confirm that the current extraction sheet is workable for the pilot and still broad enough to capture the range of care models that show up in the literature on DHTs that manage chronic disease. If we can do that without making the form unwieldy, I think we're in a good position.

turns.inner_thought: The matrix has to distinguish between real HTA-relevant evidence and papers that just gesture at broader issues. When I say full HTA coverage, I mean enough explicit material to support appraisal-style judgment across major domains, not scattered mentions. And I'm thinking of the revised spreadsheet in the shared drive, where the domains are already separated cleanly.
turns.utterance: Right. Looking at the current extraction sheet, I think the key test is whether the matrix lets us distinguish studies with full HTA coverage from studies that are essentially limited to clinical or usability outcomes. If that distinction comes through clearly in the synthesis, then the framework is doing what we need it to do.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want us to make full HTA coverage so stringent that almost every digital study looks deficient. In this literature, relevant material is often spread across methods, process evaluation, supplementary files, and implementation sections. If we credit substantive information wherever it appears, many of the better studies should count as having full HTA coverage.
turns.utterance: I agree with that as the core distinction. My only instinct is that full HTA coverage may be more visible than it first appears if we're willing to credit information wherever authors report it—main text, appendices, process sections, that kind of thing. A lot of the stronger digital studies do distribute those elements across the paper rather than presenting them in one place.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep the scope anchored on the patient-facing intervention or tightly coupled device, otherwise we drift into coding every service layer around it. For remote diabetes monitoring, the app or connected monitor is the intervention; the rest is context unless the study is explicitly about that component. If we let the boundary slide, the synthesis on DHT-specific evidence gaps will become muddy.
turns.utterance: That seems fair. On scope, though, I do think we should stay disciplined. If we take something like remote monitoring for diabetes, the review still needs to stay focused on the DHT itself rather than drifting into every surrounding service component. Otherwise the unit of analysis starts to get fuzzy quite quickly.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her concern, but in practice the digital intervention often is the service bundle. In chronic disease management, the dashboard, alerting logic, and escalation workflow can be inseparable from the patient-side tool. I don't think that broadens scope improperly; it's just what DHTs that manage chronic disease look like in real studies.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree we don't want the scope to sprawl. At the same time, for a lot of DHTs that manage chronic disease, some of those connected elements are part of what the study is actually evaluating. So I think we can stay focused while still recognising the intervention as it's presented in the paper.

turns.inner_thought: I'm relieved with the shared-drive sheet because the separate columns for ethics, interoperability, equity, and organizational impact will make underreporting visible instead of hiding it in broader notes. If we collapse those again, we'll lose the granularity needed for defensible claims in the synthesis.
turns.utterance: On the matrix itself, I'm actually fairly comfortable with the current extraction sheet as it stands. The separation across the domains should help us make underreported areas visible in the synthesis rather than folding everything into a general implementation bucket. For this review, I think that level of structure is useful.

turns.inner_thought: I think the matrix in the draft is already fairly lean, especially because implementation and organizational points sit together. I don't want reviewers dealing with too many fine-grained fields before we've tested usability. Better to keep it manageable in the pilot and then split fields later if needed.
turns.utterance: I think that's reasonable. The current extraction sheet already feels light enough for reviewers to use without too much burden, and I'd be keen to preserve that. My main concern is just making sure the pilot doesn't become cumbersome if people are trying to parse very similar kinds of contextual information in too many separate places.

turns.inner_thought: This is exactly why I want the guidance settled before launch. If the pilot starts surfacing major conceptual disagreements, we'll waste time and undermine reliability. Ready for pilot next week should mean we're past the stage of deciding what categories mean and mostly checking consistency of application.
turns.utterance: Yes, and that links to timing. If we're saying this is ready for pilot next week, I would really prefer the coding guidance to be basically settled before we start. I'd like disagreements in the pilot to reflect ambiguity in the papers, not ambiguity in the framework.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine to me because I still see the pilot as the place where we smooth edge cases. We don't need perfect stability beforehand, just enough agreement to begin applying it. And seeing how full HTA coverage appears across messy real-world studies will help us refine the boundaries pragmatically.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me. I do think the pilot will still be useful for smoothing a few category edges once we see how full HTA coverage shows up in real-world studies of DHTs that manage chronic disease. But yes, we should go in with guidance that is clear enough for reviewers to use consistently.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll treat this as approval of the revised spreadsheet in the shared folder and only make light wording edits, not structural changes. I want the review to be able to say where studies are not HTA-complete in a serious sense, so the language should point reviewers toward explicit evidence rather than casual mention.
turns.utterance: In that case, I'm happy to proceed with the current design. I'll make a few wording tweaks to the matrix in the draft and to the coding notes so we're well positioned to characterise where the literature is, and isn't, HTA-complete. I don't think we need any major redesign before the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then we can launch using the protocol version I've been working from and test it on a broad spread of intervention types, including the more service-embedded digital models. If the pilot reveals that some categories need splitting or tightening, that's exactly what it's for.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Let's launch the pilot using the current matrix and make sure the sample includes a good spread of DHTs that manage chronic disease, so we can test how the framework performs across different intervention types. That should give us enough signal to refine anything minor while keeping the timeline moving.
